zin: What if you were Mustafa Kemal Ataturk?
You'd lose your father at seven, and your hometown to a war.
You'd stop an invasion at Gallipoli, and a piece of shrapnel would hit your pocket watch instead of your heart.
You'd build a brand-new country from the ruins of an empire, and change its alphabet in a few months.
And every year, at five past nine, a whole nation would still stop for you.
So how does a boy from Salonica become the father of the Turks?
You're born in 1881, in Salonica, a busy port city of the Ottoman Empire.
Today that city is called Thessaloniki, and it lies in Greece.
Nobody writes down your birthday, so later in life you'll pick one yourself.
For now, your name is simply Mustafa.
Your father, Ali Riza, is a customs officer who later tries his luck in the timber trade.
Your mother, Zubeyde, is deeply religious, and wants you at the old school next to the mosque.
Your father wants a modern school, with desks, maps and a blackboard.
They compromise: a few days at the old school, then off to the new one.
When you're about seven, your father dies.
The money runs out, and you're sent to your uncle's farm, to chase crows off the bean fields.
Your mother worries, because you're growing up without any school at all.
But you've seen the officers in the streets of Salonica, in their sharp uniforms.
And you know exactly what you want to be.
At twelve, you take the entrance exam for the military school, without telling your mother.
You pass, and she has no choice but to accept it.
You're brilliant at maths, so good that you sometimes help the teacher.
According to the story, your maths teacher gives you a second name: Kemal, which means perfection.
From now on, you're Mustafa Kemal.
At the military high school in Monastir, you learn French and fall in love with poetry and the French Revolution.
In 1899, you move to the War College in Istanbul, the capital of the empire.
The empire is old and weak, and people in Europe call it the sick man of Europe.
The Sultan has spies everywhere, and many books are forbidden.
You read them anyway, and you even start a secret student newspaper.
In 1905, you graduate as a staff captain, but the police arrest you for your secret meetings.
Soon after, they send you far away, to an army post in Damascus.
There, you start a secret society with a few friends, called Homeland and Freedom.
In 1908, a group of young officers forces the Sultan to bring back the constitution.
They're called the Young Turks, and you know them well, but they don't really trust you.
In 1911, Italy invades Libya, the empire's last province in Africa.
You travel there in secret, through Egypt, disguised as a journalist.
In the desert near Tobruk, you organise local fighters against the Italians.
But while you're away, a much bigger disaster happens at home.
In 1912, the Balkan states attack, and the empire loses almost all its land in Europe.
Your hometown, Salonica, is handed to Greece without a fight.
Your mother and your sister flee to Istanbul as refugees.
Then you're sent to Sofia, in Bulgaria, as a military attache, where you go to balls and learn to dance.
When the First World War begins, the empire joins Germany's side.
You think it's a terrible mistake.
In 1915, Britain and France want to sail straight to Istanbul and knock the empire out of the war.
First, their warships try to force their way through the Dardanelles strait, and they fail.
So on the twenty-fifth of April, they land troops on the Gallipoli peninsula: British, French, Australians and New Zealanders.
You're a lieutenant colonel with a division in reserve, and you see the enemy climbing the hills.
The soldiers in front of you are running back, out of ammunition.
You tell them to fix their bayonets and lie down, and the enemy stops too.
Then you give your most famous order, to the fifty-seventh regiment.
I don't order you to attack. I order you to die.
In the time it takes us to die, other troops and commanders can take our place.
Almost the whole regiment is killed, but the line holds.
For eight months, both armies fight from trenches, sometimes only a few metres apart.
In August, a piece of shrapnel hits you right in the chest.
But it hits the pocket watch in your breast pocket, and you walk away with a bruise.
In January 1916, the Allies give up and sail away.
Hundreds of thousands of soldiers on both sides have been killed or wounded.
Words attributed to you are carved in stone there today: to us, there is no difference between the Johnnies and the Mehmets.
You're a hero now, and at thirty-five, you become a general: Mustafa Kemal Pasha.
But in 1918, the empire loses the war anyway.
Allied warships sail into Istanbul and anchor in front of the Sultan's palace.
According to tradition, you look at them and say: they will leave the way they came.
The winners start dividing the empire between the British, the French, the Italians and the Greeks.
In May 1919, Greek troops land in Izmir, on the west coast.
The Sultan only wants to keep his throne, and he does what the occupiers say.
So he sends you to the Black Sea, to break up what's left of the army there.
On the nineteenth of May 1919, you step ashore in Samsun, from a tired old steamship.
And you do the exact opposite of your orders.
You travel from town to town, sending telegrams and gathering officers and ordinary people.
The nation's independence, you write, will be saved by the nation's own will.
The Sultan orders you back, so you resign from the army.
Then the Sultan's government sentences you to death.
In April 1920, you open a new parliament in Ankara, a small, dusty town in the middle of Anatolia.
That summer, the Sultan signs the Treaty of Sevres, which would leave the Turks only a small piece of their own land.
Now there are two governments, and you lead the one that fights back.
The Greek army marches deeper and deeper into Anatolia, toward Ankara.
Your army is short of everything: guns, boots and food.
Women carry shells to the front, on ox carts and on their own backs.
In August 1921, you're made commander-in-chief, but you fall from your horse and break a rib.
You command anyway, in pain, from a map table near the Sakarya river.
You tell your men: there is no line of defence, there is a surface of defence, and that surface is the whole country.
The battle lasts twenty-two days and nights.
Then the Greek army turns back.
Parliament makes you a marshal, and gives you the title Gazi, the veteran.
For a whole year, you rebuild the army in silence.
Then, on the twenty-sixth of August 1922, you attack.
Within days, the enemy front breaks.
And you give your next order: armies, your first goal is the Mediterranean. Forward!
On the ninth of September, your cavalry rides into Izmir.
The war is won.
In November 1922, parliament abolishes the sultanate, after more than six hundred years.
The last Sultan leaves Istanbul quietly, on a British warship.
In 1923, the Treaty of Lausanne recognises the borders of a new Turkey.
That same year, you marry Latife, a young woman who studied law in Europe.
She travels with you and stands at your side in public, which surprises a lot of people.
But the marriage lasts only two and a half years.
On the twenty-ninth of October 1923, the Republic of Turkey is proclaimed.
Ankara becomes the capital, and you become the first president.
A few months later, you abolish the caliphate as well.
Now you want to change everything, and fast.
In 1925, men have to stop wearing the fez, and wear hats instead.
You show them how, by touring the country in a Panama hat.
New laws, based on European ones, give women equal rights in marriage and divorce.
Then, in 1928, the biggest change of all: the Arabic letters are replaced by a new Latin alphabet.
You travel from town to town with a chalkboard, and teach the new letters yourself.
People start calling you the head teacher.
In 1934, Turkish women get the right to vote and to be elected, earlier than in France or Italy.
That same year, everyone in Turkey has to choose a surname.
Parliament gives you yours: Ataturk, Father of the Turks, and nobody else is allowed to use it.
Your adopted daughter, Sabiha Gokcen, becomes one of the first female fighter pilots in the world.
But it all happens under one party, yours, and revolts against your reforms are put down hard.
Your motto for the world is simple: peace at home, peace in the world.
But years of hard work and little sleep wear you down, and your liver is failing.
In 1938, you lie sick in Dolmabahce Palace, on the water in Istanbul.
On the tenth of November, at five past nine in the morning, you die, at fifty-seven.
According to tradition, the clock in your room is stopped at that exact minute.
Hundreds of thousands of people line the streets to say goodbye.
Today, you rest in Anitkabir, a huge mausoleum on a hill in Ankara.
Your face is on every banknote, and your portrait hangs in schools and offices.
And every tenth of November, at exactly five past nine, sirens sound.
Cars stop on the highway, people step out, and the whole country stands still.
